question:
Choose the word that is opposite in meaning to the given word.
Pliable
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Rigid.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Pliable" means easily bent or shaped; flexible, or easily influenced/adaptable. (लचीला)
◦ Example: Willow branches are pliable and can be woven into baskets.

• Its exact opposite is "Rigid", meaning stiff and inflexible; not able to be bent, moved, or changed easily. (कठोर, अनम्य)
◦ Example: The steel rod was too rigid to bend by hand.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Fluid" (तरल, प्रवाही): Able to flow easily, or likely to change shape/form readily — this is close in meaning to "pliable", not its opposite.

• Option 3: "Variable" (परिवर्तनशील): Likely to change or vary; not fixed or constant — again a near-synonym of "pliable" in the sense of adaptability.

• Option 4: "Ductile" (तन्य, आसानी से ढलने वाला): Capable of being drawn into wires, or (of a person) easily led/moulded — a near-synonym of "pliable", not an antonym.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "Pliable": flexible, supple, malleable, adaptable, compliant, docile.

• Other common antonym pairs tested by SSC: Rigid × Flexible/Elastic, Stiff × Supple, Obstinate × Pliant.

question:
Rearrange the parts of the sentence in correct order.
From the
P. California to the pork hub of China,
Q. reduced food supplies and sharply increased food prices
R. grain heartland of Argentina to the tomato belt of
S. extreme weather events in 2021 have
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. RPSQ.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The fixed opener "From the" must be followed by a noun phrase, so it connects naturally with R ("grain heartland of Argentina to the tomato belt of"), since "From the" + "grain heartland" forms a grammatical start.

• Part R ends with "tomato belt of", which needs a place name to complete it — this is supplied by P ("California to the pork hub of China,"), giving the parallel "from...to...to...to..." structure covering four regions/products.

• After the comma in P, the subject of the main clause is needed — S ("extreme weather events in 2021 have") supplies the subject "extreme weather events" and the auxiliary "have".

• Finally, Q ("reduced food supplies and sharply increased food prices") completes the predicate after the auxiliary "have".

• Reading it in full: "From the grain heartland of Argentina to the tomato belt of California to the pork hub of China, extreme weather events in 2021 have reduced food supplies and sharply increased food prices." This is grammatically complete and logically coherent.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 (RPQS) is incorrect because it places the subject-verb group S after the object Q, breaking the sentence — "...pork hub of China, reduced food supplies... extreme weather events in 2021 have" makes no sense.

• Option 3 (QPRS) is incorrect because it starts with the predicate Q right after "From the", which is ungrammatical, since "From the" needs a noun phrase, not a verb phrase.

• Option 4 (SPQR) is incorrect because it places the subject-verb group S immediately after "From the", which is not grammatical, and it leaves the sentence without a proper concluding phrase.

NOTE

• In sentence-rearrangement questions, first identify the part that logically connects to any fixed opening/closing fragment, then look for grammatical cues such as prepositions needing a noun phrase, or a comma indicating a clause boundary.

• Parallel structures using repeated prepositions ("from...to...to...") are a strong clue to the correct sequencing of listed items.

question:
Select the word that is closest in meaning (SYNONYM) to the word given below.
Dreary
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Dull.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Dreary" means dull, gloomy, bleak, and lacking excitement or interest. (उदास, नीरस)
◦ Example: It was a dreary, rainy afternoon with nothing to do.

• Its closest synonym among the options is "Dull", which also means lacking brightness, interest, or excitement. (नीरस, फीका)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Faith" (विश्वास): Means trust or belief; unrelated to "dreary".

• Option 3: "Superstitious" (अंधविश्वासी): Means believing in superstition; unrelated in meaning.

• Option 4: "Active" (सक्रिय): Means energetic and lively — in fact nearly opposite to the gloomy sense of "dreary".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "Dreary": bleak, dismal, gloomy, monotonous, drab, cheerless.

• Antonyms of "Dreary": cheerful, lively, bright, exciting.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
While one cannot really say the pandemic is over yet, it is a sensible decision to now ________ to the older system.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Revert.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The verb "Revert (to)" means to return to a former state, practice, or system. (पूर्व स्थिति में लौटना)
◦ Example: After the trial period ended, the company reverted to its old pricing policy.

• The sentence talks about going back to "the older system" once the pandemic situation eases, which exactly matches the meaning of "revert to".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Sympathise" (सहानुभूति रखना): Means to feel or express sympathy/compassion for someone; it does not fit the context of returning to a system.

• Option 2: "Comprehend" (समझना): Means to understand; it does not convey the sense of "going back to".

• Option 4: "Stick" (टिके रहना): Normally used as "stick to" meaning to continue with something already being followed, not to "go back" to an older, discontinued system — so it does not fit as precisely as "revert to".

NOTE

• Common confusion pair: "revert to" (go back to an earlier state) vs "refer to" (to mention or consult).

• Other useful synonyms of "revert": relapse, return, regress, resume (an earlier state).

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Piece of cake
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Something which is very simple.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Piece of cake" means a task or activity that is very easy to do. (बहुत आसान काम)
◦ Example: Don't worry about the test, it will be a piece of cake for you.

• The idiom draws on the idea that eating a piece of cake requires no effort at all, hence anything described this way is effortless.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Extremely difficult is the opposite meaning; this would instead be expressed by idioms like "a tough nut to crack" or "an uphill task".

• Option 3: Intuition for something dangerous is unrelated; a sense of danger would be expressed as "to smell a rat" or "to sense trouble".

• Option 4: Invitation for birthday is a literal, unrelated meaning and has nothing to do with the idiomatic sense.

NOTE

• Other idioms meaning "very easy": "A walk in the park", "Child's play", "As easy as ABC", "A cakewalk".

• Idioms meaning "very difficult" (often confused as opposites in exams): "A tough nut to crack", "An uphill task", "A hard nut to crack".

question:
Choose the word that means the same as the given word.
Ecclesial
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Churchly.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Ecclesial" means relating to a church or churches; of or belonging to the church. (गिरजाघर संबंधी, चर्च से जुड़ा हुआ)
◦ Example: The bishop spoke about the ecclesial duties of the newly ordained priests.

• Its closest synonym among the options is "Churchly", meaning appropriate to or characteristic of a church. (चर्च से संबंधित)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Profane" (अपवित्र): Means showing disrespect for sacred things, or secular/non-religious — nearly opposite to "ecclesial".

• Option 2: "Secular" (धर्मनिरपेक्ष): Means not connected with religious or spiritual matters — the direct opposite of "ecclesial".

• Option 3: "Profuse" (प्रचुर): Means abundant or plentiful; unrelated in meaning to "ecclesial".

NOTE

• Related words: ecclesiastical (also means "relating to the church", often used for church hierarchy/clergy), ecclesiology (study of church doctrine).

• Common antonym pair often tested: Ecclesial/Ecclesiastical × Secular/Profane.

question:
Fill in the blank with an appropriate option.
Choosing the right software for any purpose can be a/an ________ task for any business.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Challenging.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The adjective "Challenging" means testing one's abilities; difficult in a way that requires effort and skill. (चुनौतीपूर्ण)
◦ Example: Managing a large team remotely can be a challenging task.

• The sentence talks about the difficulty involved in choosing the right software, which is best described by "challenging".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Intimating" (सूचित करना): Means announcing or making known; it is not used to describe a difficult task, and does not fit grammatically here.

• Option 3: "Flickering" (टिमटिमाना): Means shining unsteadily or wavering, typically used for light or flames; irrelevant to a "task".

• Option 4: "Attributing" (जिम्मेदार ठहराना): Means regarding something as being caused by something else; it does not describe the nature of a task.

NOTE

• Words close in meaning to "challenging" in exams: demanding, taxing, arduous, exacting.

• Words that are commonly confused with "challenging" due to similar spelling patterns: "chilling", "changing" — always read the full context before choosing.

question:
In the following question, out of the given four alternatives, select the alternative which best expresses the meaning of the Idiom/Phrase.
To breast the tape
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. To win a race.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "To breast the tape" means to win a race. (दौड़ जीतना)
◦ Example: The young athlete breasted the tape well ahead of the other runners to clinch the gold medal.

• The idiom comes from athletics, where the winner of a race is the first runner to touch (breast) the finishing tape stretched across the track.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: To shut someone's mouth (किसी को चुप कराना): Means to stop someone from talking; unrelated to "breast the tape".

• Option 2: To create problems (समस्याएँ खड़ी करना): Means to cause trouble; unrelated in meaning.

• Option 3: To bring joy (खुशी लाना): Means to make someone happy; not the meaning of this idiom.

NOTE

• Other racing/sports-derived idioms often tested by SSC: "To win by a whisker" (win by a very narrow margin), "To be neck and neck" (very close competition), "To throw in the towel" (to give up).

question:
Find the part of the given sentence that has an error in it. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
There is evidence that much too technology can lead to a loss of child development opportunities.
option_4: There is evidence that much too
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. There is evidence that much too.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The error lies in the word order "much too technology". When "much" and "too" are used together to modify a noun in the sense of excess quantity, the correct order is "too much", not "much too".

• Rule: "Too much" is used before an uncountable noun to mean "an excessive amount of" (e.g., too much technology, too much noise). "Much too" is instead used before an adjective/adverb to intensify it (e.g., much too expensive, much too loud) — it cannot directly modify a noun like "technology".

• The corrected sentence should read: "There is evidence that too much technology can lead to a loss of child development opportunities."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: No error is incorrect because an error does exist, as explained above.

• Option 2: "technology can lead to a" is grammatically correct in itself and contains no error.

• Option 3: "loss of child development opportunities." is grammatically correct and contains no error.

NOTE

• Remember the distinction: "too much/too many" + noun (too much water, too many chairs) versus "much too" + adjective/adverb (much too hot, much too quickly).

• "Too many" is used before plural countable nouns, while "too much" is used before uncountable nouns.

question:
Some parts of a few sentences have been jumbled up, and labelled A, B, C and D. Select the option that gives the correct sequence in which these parts can be rearranged to form a meaningful and grammatically correct sentence.
I knew that the remedy lay not
A. let the past go. Be at ease. Allow the future
B. Rohan had advised me over and again:
C. to arrive at its own pace
D. in finding a new flower but in what unfurling its secrets when it will.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. DBAC.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The fixed opener "I knew that the remedy lay not" requires a continuation of the idea of what the remedy did NOT lie in — this is supplied by D ("in finding a new flower but in what unfurling its secrets when it will."), which completes the "not...but..." contrast.

• After this reflective statement, B ("Rohan had advised me over and again:") introduces, with a colon, the advice that is about to be quoted.

• The colon in B is completed by the quoted advice in A ("let the past go. Be at ease. Allow the future").

• Part A ends mid-thought with "Allow the future", which is grammatically completed by C ("to arrive at its own pace"), forming the full instruction "Allow the future to arrive at its own pace."

• Reading it in full: "I knew that the remedy lay not in finding a new flower but in what unfurling its secrets when it will. Rohan had advised me over and again: let the past go. Be at ease. Allow the future to arrive at its own pace." This flows logically and is grammatically complete.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 (DACB) is incorrect because it places A (the quoted advice) before B (the introduction to the quote with the colon), reversing the logical order.

• Option 3 (CDBA) is incorrect because it starts with C ("to arrive at its own pace"), which cannot directly follow the opener "I knew that the remedy lay not", as it is a dangling infinitive phrase with no context yet.

• Option 4 (ACDB) is incorrect because it places the quoted advice A immediately after the opener, before Rohan's advice has even been introduced by B.

NOTE

• In parts jumbled with a colon (:), always look for the part ending with the colon — it must be followed immediately by the part that logically completes/quotes it.

• Watch for split phrases (like "Allow the future" / "to arrive at its own pace") — these must always stay adjacent and in the correct order.

question:
Identify the segment in the sentence which contains a grammatical error, then select the option "No error".
The London-based Brodsky/ Quartet, meanwhile, is one of/ the world's leading string quartet.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. the world's leading string quartet.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rule: The construction "one of the + plural noun" always requires a plural countable noun, since it refers to one item selected from among several of that same kind.

• In the given sentence, "is one of the world's leading string quartet" wrongly uses the singular noun "quartet". It should be the plural "quartets", giving "...is one of the world's leading string quartets."

• This segment, "the world's leading string quartet.", therefore contains the grammatical error.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "The London-based Brodsky" is grammatically correct; it is simply an adjectival phrase modifying "Quartet".

• Option 3: "Quartet, meanwhile, is one of" is grammatically correct; the singular subject "Quartet" correctly takes the singular verb "is".

• Option 4: "No error" is incorrect because an error does exist, as explained above.

NOTE

• Always apply "one of the + plural noun (+ singular verb if it is the main subject)": e.g., "He is one of the best players." NOT "He is one of the best player."

• Do not confuse this with "one of the + plural noun + who/that + plural verb" constructions, e.g., "He is one of the boys who play football," where the relative clause verb agrees with the plural noun, not with "one".

question:
Select the correct passive form of the given sentence.
Swallows build new nests every year.
option_1: New nests were built by swallows every year.
option_2: New nests are built by swallows every year.
option_3: New nests were being built by swallows every year.
option_4: New nests is being built by swallows every year.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. New nests are built by swallows every year.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "Swallows build new nests every year" is an assertive sentence in the Simple Present Tense.

• Rule — Simple Present Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + V1/V5 + Object
◦ Passive: Object + is/am/are + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule: the object "new nests" becomes the subject "new nests"; it is plural, so the auxiliary is "are"; the verb "build" becomes the past participle "built"; and "swallows" becomes the agent with "by".
◦ Passive: New nests are built by swallows every year.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "were built" is the passive of the Simple Past Tense, not the Simple Present Tense used in the active sentence.

• Option 3 is incorrect because "were being built" is the passive of the Past Continuous Tense.

• Option 4 is incorrect because the subject "New nests" is plural but the verb "is" is singular, violating subject-verb agreement.

NOTE

• The time expression "every year" is itself a strong signal of the Simple Present Tense, both in active and passive voice.

• Always check subject-verb agreement (singular/plural) carefully in passive-voice options, as SSC frequently sets traps like Option 4.

question: Select the correctly spelt word
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Amateur.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Amateur" — a person who engages in an activity, especially a sport, on an unpaid basis rather than professionally.
◦ Example: He remained a proud amateur golfer throughout his life, never turning professional.

• Spelling key: A + M + A + T + E + U + R. Note the sequence "teur" at the end. The word comes from French amateur, ultimately from Latin amator ("lover"), related to "amare" (to love).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Amatuer" — incorrect; the "u" and "e" before the final "r" have been interchanged.

• Option 2: "Amatueer" — incorrect; contains an extra, misplaced "e" giving a wrong ending.

• Option 3: "Amture" — incorrect; the letter "a" after "Am" has been dropped, and the ending is malformed.

NOTE

• The related noun is amateurism, and the antonym is professional.

• Other French-origin words with tricky endings: connoisseur, entrepreneur, chauffeur, saboteur, restaurateur.

question: Select the correctly spelt word
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Reprimand.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Reprimand" — a formal or official statement of disapproval or rebuke; also used as a verb meaning to rebuke someone formally.
◦ Example: The officer was given a stern reprimand for his negligence.

• Spelling key: RE + PRI + MAND. Note the vowel "i" in the middle syllable "pri" and the ending "-mand" (not "-ment" or "-mend" or "-mant").

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Repriment" — incorrect; the middle vowel "i" has been dropped/altered and the ending wrongly changed to "-ment".

• Option 3: "Reprimend" — incorrect; the ending has been wrongly changed to "-mend" instead of "-mand".

• Option 4: "Reprimant" — incorrect; the ending has been wrongly changed to "-mant" instead of "-mand".

NOTE

• Do not confuse "reprimand" with "amend" or "comment", which have genuinely similar-looking endings but are different words.

• Other words often confused for their endings: recommend, command, demand — all end in "-mand/-mend" but must be memorised individually.

question:
Choose the option that is the correct direct form of the sentence.
The teacher asked me if I had seen the match.
option_1: "Did you see the match?" the teacher said to me.
option_2: "Did you had saw the match?" the teacher said to me.
option_3: "Did you saw the match?" the teacher said to me.
option_4: "Did you seen the match?" the teacher said to me.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. "Did you see the match?" the teacher said to me.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rule — Narration (reverse backshift of tense): When converting reported (indirect) speech back into direct speech, a tense that has been backshifted in the indirect version must be shifted back to its original, simpler form in the direct version.

• In the given indirect sentence, the reported verb is in the Past Perfect Tense ("had seen"). When a question was originally asked in the Simple Past Tense, it becomes Past Perfect Tense on conversion to indirect speech. Reversing this, the direct question must be in the Simple Past Tense: "Did you see the match?"

• Since the indirect sentence is an "if/whether" question (an interrogative sentence reported with "asked...if"), the direct version must be framed as a direct question, ending with a question mark, exactly as in Option 1.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Did you had saw the match?" is incorrect because it wrongly mixes the auxiliary "did" with "had" and the past participle "saw" — this is not standard English question formation.

• Option 3: "Did you saw the match?" is incorrect because after the auxiliary "did", the base form of the verb must be used ("see"), not the past form "saw".

• Option 4: "Did you seen the match?" is incorrect for the same reason — after "did", the base form "see" is required, not the past participle "seen".

NOTE

• Always remember: with the auxiliary "did", the main verb must be in its base (V1) form — this is the most common trap in such questions.

• In yes/no reported questions ("if/whether"), the direct version always restores the subject-auxiliary inversion and the question mark.

question:
Improve the underlined part of the sentence. Choose 'No improvement' as an answer if the sentence is grammatically correct.
I can't concentrate on my work because I am thinking off that beautiful scene.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. am thinking about.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rule: The verb "think" when used in the sense of "to have someone/something in one's mind" is followed by the preposition "about" or "of", not by "off", which is an incorrect homophone-based error here.

• The subject "I" and the context ("can't concentrate... because I ___ that beautiful scene") require the Present Continuous Tense, which must remain as "am thinking", correctly matching the subject "I".

• Correcting only the faulty preposition "off" to "about" gives the grammatically correct sentence: "I can't concentrate on my work because I am thinking about that beautiful scene."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "was think of" is incorrect because "was think" is not a valid verb form (it should be "was thinking" for past continuous), and it also wrongly changes the tense from present to past, which does not fit the context of "can't concentrate" (present tense).

• Option 3: "is thinking about" is incorrect because the auxiliary "is" does not agree with the subject "I" (which requires "am").

• Option 4: "No improvement" is incorrect because the original sentence does contain an error — "thinking off" is not correct usage.

NOTE

• Common preposition confusions in SSC exams: "think of/about" (correct) vs "think off" (incorrect, sounds like "thinking of" but is wrong); "switch off" (correct, different verb).

• Always check subject-verb (auxiliary) agreement first in "improve the sentence" questions — a common trap is changing the tense unnecessarily, as in Option 1.

question:
Select the word that is closest in meaning (SYNONYM) to the word given below.
UNBIASED
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Candid.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Unbiased" means showing no prejudice; impartial and fair, giving an honest and objective view. (निष्पक्ष)
◦ Example: The judge gave an unbiased verdict, free from any personal prejudice.

• Its closest synonym among the options is "Candid", meaning truthful, straightforward, and free from bias or hidden motives in expressing an opinion. (स्पष्टवादी, निष्कपट)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Uncomplaining" (बिना शिकायत किए): Means not complaining, enduring hardship patiently — unrelated to impartiality.

• Option 3: "Sapient" (बुद्धिमान): Means wise or having great wisdom — unrelated to being unbiased.

• Option 4: "Humble" (विनम्र): Means modest, not proud — unrelated to fairness or impartiality.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "Unbiased": impartial, neutral, objective, fair-minded, even-handed.

• Antonyms of "Unbiased": biased, prejudiced, partial, one-sided.

question:
Given below are four jumbled sentences. Pick the option that gives their correct order.
P. Amongst all the cities of Japan, Hiroshima is the one that experiences earliest mornings.
Q. It experiences the earliest sun rise amongst all the countries.
R. According to the words of the Japanese envoy himself, that name was chosen because the country was so close to where the sun rises.
S. Japan is also known as the land of the rising sun.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. SQRP.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The topic must be introduced first: S ("Japan is also known as the land of the rising sun.") is the logical opening sentence, introducing Japan's nickname.

• Q ("It experiences the earliest sun rise amongst all the countries.") naturally follows S, using the pronoun "It" to refer back to "Japan" and explaining why it is called the "land of the rising sun".

• R ("According to the words of the Japanese envoy himself, that name was chosen because the country was so close to where the sun rises.") follows next, elaborating on the origin of the name "land of the rising sun" mentioned in S/Q.

• P ("Amongst all the cities of Japan, Hiroshima is the one that experiences earliest mornings.") logically concludes the paragraph, narrowing the focus from the whole country to a specific city, Hiroshima.

• Reading it in full: "Japan is also known as the land of the rising sun. It experiences the earliest sun rise amongst all the countries. According to the words of the Japanese envoy himself, that name was chosen because the country was so close to where the sun rises. Amongst all the cities of Japan, Hiroshima is the one that experiences earliest mornings." This flows logically from general (the country) to specific (a city).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 (SRQP) is incorrect because it places R (explaining the origin of the name) before Q (which first states the fact that needs explaining), breaking the logical flow.

• Option 2 (PSQR) is incorrect because it starts with P, which discusses a specific city (Hiroshima) before the country-level context (Japan, the rising sun) has even been introduced.

• Option 3 (QPRS) is incorrect because it starts with Q, whose pronoun "It" has no antecedent without S coming first.

NOTE

• In para-jumble questions, always identify the sentence that introduces the main topic/subject (usually without any pronoun referring backward) as the likely opening sentence.

• Track pronouns ("it", "that", "this") carefully — they must refer to something already mentioned in a preceding sentence.

question:
Select the option that will improve the underlined part of the sentence. In case no improvement is needed, select 'No improvement'.
Neither of the two companies are winning in the price war.
option_1: Neither of two company is winning
option_2: Neither of the companies are winning
option_3: Neither of the two companies is winning
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Neither of the two companies is winning.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rule: "Neither" and "Either" are singular indefinite pronouns; when used as the subject of a sentence (as in "Neither of the two companies..."), they must always take a singular verb, regardless of the plural noun that follows "of".

• In the given sentence, "Neither of the two companies are winning" wrongly uses the plural verb "are". This must be corrected to the singular "is winning", giving "Neither of the two companies is winning in the price war."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Neither of two company is winning" is incorrect because after "of", the noun must be both plural ("companies", not "company") and preceded by "the" when referring to two specific, already-identified companies.

• Option 2: "Neither of the companies are winning" is incorrect because it still uses the plural verb "are" with "Neither", which requires a singular verb.

• Option 4: "No improvement" is incorrect because the original sentence does contain a subject-verb agreement error, as explained above.

NOTE

• Other words that always take a singular verb as subject: each, either, neither, everyone, someone, nobody, anybody.

• Example: "Either of the two roads leads to the station." (NOT "lead").

question:
Fill in the blank with an appropriate option.
Do you ______ your tap water before drinking?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Filter.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The verb "Filter" means to pass a liquid or gas through a device to remove unwanted solid particles or impurities. (छानना, फ़िल्टर करना)
◦ Example: Many households filter their tap water before drinking it to remove impurities.

• Since the sentence is asking about treating tap water before drinking, "filter" is the only word that fits this specific context of water purification.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Flush" (बहा देना/साफ़ करना): Means to clean something by causing water to flow through it, or to force liquid rapidly out; it does not fit "tap water before drinking".

• Option 3: "Flirt" (छेड़खानी करना): Means to behave playfully/romantically towards someone; completely unrelated to water.

• Option 4: "Flicker" (टिमटिमाना): Means to shine or burn unsteadily, typically used for light; irrelevant to water treatment.

NOTE

• Commonly confused near-homophone words tested by SSC: flush/filter/flick/flirt/flicker — always check the meaning that fits the specific context of the sentence, not just similar sound or spelling.

• Related vocabulary: purify, filtrate, strain, decontaminate — all relate to removing impurities from a substance.

Generally, dolphins sleep (1) ________ only one brain hemisphere in slow-wave sleep at a time, thus (2) ________ enough consciousness to breathe and to watch for possible (3) ________ and other threats. Early (4) ________ stages can occur simultaneously in both hemispheres. In captivity, dolphins seemingly enter a fully asleep state where both eyes are closed and there is no response to mild external (5) ________.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank No.1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. with.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rule: The preposition "with" is used to indicate the means, instrument, or faculty used to perform an action — here, dolphins sleep "with" only one brain hemisphere active, meaning they use only that hemisphere for sleeping at a time.

• The correct sentence reads: "Generally, dolphins sleep with only one brain hemisphere in slow-wave sleep at a time...", which correctly conveys that only one hemisphere is engaged in sleep at any given time.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "on" does not fit; "sleep on" would suggest a surface or location, not a means/instrument, and does not make sense with "brain hemisphere".

• Option 3: "over" does not fit the sense of using a specific body part/faculty to perform the sleeping action.

• Option 4: "through" would suggest passing through something, which does not match the intended meaning of using only one hemisphere.

NOTE

• Prepositions in cloze passages must be chosen based on the precise sense conveyed in context — always read the full sentence, not just the blank, to determine which preposition fits logically.

• "With" commonly indicates the means/tool/faculty by which an action is performed, e.g., "write with a pen", "see with one's eyes".

Additional Information

NOTE

• Words close to "maintaining" in this sense: sustaining, retaining, preserving, keeping up.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank No.3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. predators.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rule: The blank must be a plural noun that pairs naturally with "and other threats", since the dolphin watches for possible danger while sleeping.

• The correct sentence reads: "...to watch for possible predators and other threats", where "predators" (animals that hunt and kill other animals for food) are a natural, direct threat that a sleeping dolphin would need to remain alert for.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "preys" is grammatically odd here ("prey" is typically used as an uncountable/collective noun, and "preys" as a plural is unusual), and conceptually a dolphin watches out for creatures that might attack it (predators), not for its own prey while sleeping.

• Option 3: "carnivorous" is an adjective (meaning "meat-eating"), not a noun, so it cannot grammatically fill a blank that requires a noun paired with "and other threats".

• Option 4: "orators" means public speakers, which is completely unrelated to the context of animal threats.

NOTE

• Word-form (part of speech) checks are essential in cloze passages — a grammatically wrong part of speech, like the adjective "carnivorous" in Option 3, can be eliminated immediately.

• "Predator" (noun, hunter) versus "prey" (noun, hunted) is a commonly tested word pair in vocabulary and comprehension questions.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank No.5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. stimuli.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rule: The blank requires a plural noun following "mild external ________", referring to outside signals or triggers that would normally cause a response in a living creature.

• The correct sentence reads: "...there is no response to mild external stimuli", where "stimuli" (the plural of "stimulus") means things that provoke or evoke a reaction — here, the deeply asleep dolphin does not react to such mild outside triggers.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "moduli" is the plural of "modulus" (a mathematical/technical term), which is completely unrelated to a biological response context.

• Option 3: "spur" means a thing that prompts or encourages an action; while related in idea, it does not naturally collocate with "external" and "response to" the way "stimuli" does, and is not typically used in the plural sense demanded here.

• Option 4: "deterrent" means something that discourages an action; it does not fit the sense of "response to external ________", which requires a neutral term for an external signal/trigger.

NOTE

• "Stimulus" (singular) / "stimuli" (plural) is a commonly tested irregular Latin plural — similar irregular plurals include: syllabus/syllabi, cactus/cacti, phenomenon/phenomena, criterion/criteria.

• In biology/psychology contexts, "stimulus-response" is a standard collocation describing how organisms react to external triggers.
